title: Roadside Checks & Prohibitions
whatItIs: The police and DVSA can stop lorries to check weights, roadworthiness, tachograph records and licences. A prohibition stops you driving until the problem is fixed.

keyFacts.text: You MUST stop when a uniformed DVSA officer or police officer asks you to: not stopping is an offence.

keyFacts: DVSA officers wear yellow jackets with the DVSA logo and always carry a DVSA warrant card.
A vehicle with a trailer is treated as 2 units, so you could get more than one prohibition.
You can be fined £50 to £300, or taken to court for more serious offences. Defective brakes: £100 and 3 points.

visual.caption: Delayed prohibitions: time to get defects fixed

rows: More than 1 defect in a safety critical area
1 defect in a safety critical area, or 5 or more in non-critical areas
Fewer than 5 defects in non-critical areas
notes: Safety critical areas include brakes, lights and steering.
An immobilised vehicle costs £80 to release, once the issues are fixed.

a.label: Immediate prohibition
points: You can't drive until the problem is fixed

b.label: Delayed prohibition
points: You can drive away: up to 10 days to fix it

onTheTest.question: An examiner finds 1 defect in a safety critical area and issues a delayed prohibition. How long could you have to fix it?
onTheTest.why: 1 defect in a safety critical area gives 4 to 7 days. More than 1 safety critical defect gives up to 3 days.

onTheTest.question: At a roadside check your vehicle is found to be overloaded. What will you be issued with?
onTheTest.why: An overloaded vehicle gets an immediate prohibition notice and may be immobilised. Officers can direct it nearby to redistribute or remove the load.

traps: Immediate 'S' marked prohibition: the vehicle is likely to be immobilised and you could be prosecuted.
No 'S' marking for a defect you couldn't have known about, such as an underside defect.
Carrying a high-value load? Keep the engine running and doors locked until sure the officer is genuine.
